name: PT Akasha Wira International Tbk

frontmatter.title: Akasha Wira International — a quality franchise priced close to its value inside a tight float
frontmatter.summary: Akasha Wira sells bottled water, Korean-style food and salon hair care into Indonesia and has nearly doubled sales in two years on a distribution push, with no net debt and returns on equity in the high twenties. Our discounted cash flow values it well above the price, but the multiple cross-checks and an eighth-float regime pull the blended target back to the price. HOLD.
thesis: {'Two profitable franchises, not one': "bottled water and food sit beside a cosmetics range that carries most of the group's gross profit [S2]."}
{'Growth is manufactured by distribution, not declared': 'the 2025 and first-half 2026 step came from extending reach, and both segments grew together [S3].'}
{'The cash engine funds the build': 'net cash, a liquidity portfolio and capex at roughly a quarter of sales while the plants go up [S2][S0].'}
The DCF and the multiples disagree by half; the blended target sits between them, close to today's price, which is why the rating is HOLD rather than the DCF's ADD [S2][S0].
The controlled float, the HSC listing and the March 2027 free-float step cap any re-rating until the register changes [S8][S10][S13].

catalysts.event: First free-float step to the intermediate threshold, or a controller sell-down to meet it
FY2026 audited results — the first full year carrying the enlarged distribution base
MSCI consultation feedback window on Indonesia's index status closes
MSCI decision on the proposed move to Standalone status
Annual general meeting — dividend decision and board renewal

blocks.text: We initiate Akasha Wira International (ADES) at **HOLD** with a twelve-month target of **Rp32,140**, against a last price of Rp29,325 — a total return of 9.6%. The target sits on a fundamental twelve-month value of Rp31,479. Our primary discounted cash flow values the equity at Rp39,106 per share; the blended multiple cross-checks land far below that, and the weighted, liquidity-adjusted fundamental value is what the target is built on [S2][S3].

The variant view is not that the company is misunderstood — the market has clearly noticed. It is that the market is applying a de-rated Indonesian consumer multiple to a business that has just shown it can grow far faster than the category. The reverse DCF makes the disagreement precise: at today's price the market discounts FY2027E revenue growth of 17.7%, against the 22.0% we forecast. That gap is narrower than the DCF-versus-multiple spread suggests, and it is the reason we do not rate the stock ADD on the DCF alone: the market already pays 15.8x on this year's earnings, which is branded-quality territory in this peer set rather than a distressed multiple [S0].

What moves the value is narrow and identifiable. First, whether the 2026 step is repeatable: the first half of 2026 grew both segments by more than half, so the second half and FY2027 are the test [S3]. Second, capital intensity: capex is running at roughly a quarter of sales while the plants are built, and it has to fall for the cash flow to show [S2]. Third, the float. The controller holds almost the entire company, the free float sits below the new exchange minimum with a deadline inside our forecast window, and a sell-down or a new issue would each change the per-share arithmetic [S8][S10][S13]. The konglo lens in the valuation section prices that regime explicitly; it is not the reason the target sits below the DCF — the multiple weights are — but it is the reason the twelve-month path is not a straight line to fundamental value.

The multiple cross-checks disagree with the DCF by more than half, and we do not smooth that away. The method set is the house set, so the weights stand; but the report says plainly which side we believe and why the blend, not the DCF, is the honest twelve-month answer for a stock with an eighth of its shares in public hands. A quality-matched forward multiple would value ADES near the price, not at the DCF; that is a finding about the market's own pricing of the franchise, and it is why the rating is HOLD [S0].

Akasha Wira is a Jakarta-based consumer manufacturer with two reporting segments. The food and beverage segment bottles drinking water under the Nestlé Pure Life and Vica brands, sells soy milk under Pureal and has moved into Korean-style food under Mujigae and Wonhae; the cosmetics segment makes and sells the Makarizo salon hair-care range, alongside licensed Wella and Clairol products [S2][S4]. Water production started commercially in the eighties, cosmetics trading and then manufacturing followed, and food production began later still, so the group has been assembled product category by product category rather than grown from a single brand [S2].

The revenue split is close to even and that is the single most important fact about the business. In FY2025 food and beverage produced IDR1,374.6bn of net sales and cosmetics IDR1,352.3bn, out of IDR2,727.0bn for the group [S2]. But the profit split is not even: cosmetics generated IDR849.7bn of gross profit against IDR580.8bn for food and beverage, because the hair-care range earns a segment gross margin in the sixties while bottled water earns one in the low forties [S2]. Water is the volume and the distribution footprint; hair care is where the money is made. A reader who models ADES as a water company will get the margin structure wrong.

The strategy is stated as five focus areas — trusted brands, superior value, wide availability, organisational capability and cost discipline — and the annual report is explicit that the group's objective is to maximise the average annual gain in intrinsic value per share rather than to hit a reported profit line [S4]. In practice the 2025 and 2026 growth came from extending distribution reach across the islands and pushing both portfolios through it: the company says it expanded distribution for the water brands to raise penetration and entered non-bottled beverages and Korean food to reach younger consumers [S4]. Sales are entirely to third parties — there is no group sales channel dressing up the revenue line [S2].

The footprint is a domestic one with a small export tail. Production is in West Java and East Java for water, West Java for food and Bogor for cosmetics, and the geographic split of FY2025 sales was weighted heavily to Java with a much smaller outer-island book and a rounding-error export line [S2]. The headcount is remarkably small — 1,862 employees at end-2025 — which says the distribution model leans on third-party logistics and distributors rather than a captive army [S4]. That is efficient while it works and it is a dependency while it does not.

Control is absolute and traceable. Waters Partners Bottling SA held 91.35% of the shares at the end of 2025, and the chain above it runs through Sofos Pte Ltd in Singapore and Fortitude Capital Management to Andy Pe [S4]. The controlling entity was originally a Coca-Cola and Nestlé joint venture, and Sofos acquired it in 2008; the brand licences that come with that history are the subject of the governance section [S2][S4]. Akasha is therefore not part of a listed Indonesian group — it is the listed vehicle of a single private controller, which changes both the governance questions and the float arithmetic.

Bottled drinking water in Indonesia is a large, structurally growing category: the company describes demand as supported by health awareness and by a shift away from sugary ready-to-drink beverages, with the market continuing to expand in 2025 [S4]. The same disclosure is candid about the competitive structure — the category is dominated by large, well-established players including multinationals and global market leaders with scale and resources, so share is won on execution and distribution rather than on a product niche [S4]. That is the correct frame for ADES: it is a challenger in water with a national brand licence and a regional plant base, not a category leader.

Hair care is a different fight. The Makarizo brand is sold through salons as well as retail, which gives it a professional channel that mass-market shampoo brands do not own, and it is the reason the cosmetics segment earns a materially higher gross margin than water [S2]. The trade-off is dependence on that channel and on the licence: a professional hair-care franchise is only as strong as its salon relationships and its brand rights.

The drivers that matter for our forecast are therefore not commodity prices, but the cost links are not negligible either. Raw materials were IDR618.1bn of FY2025 cost of goods sold and packaging and indirect materials IDR352.9bn, so raw materials were less than half the cost base while packaging was more than a quarter [S2]. Bottling and hair-care packaging is mostly PET and HDPE, whose resin price follows the oil and palm-derived monomer complex: taking resin at roughly two-fifths of packaging cost puts the palm-linked slice of the cost base near an eighth rather than the small fraction an earlier draft assumed. We therefore model the palm link at that level. It still barely moves the forecast, because the house agri deck's CPO path for FY2027E sits only a few per cent above spot: at twice our modelled link the FY2027E gross-margin effect is about half a point, and at three times it is about a point, with most of the cost passed through. That is small enough that the base case does not hinge on the exact link, and large enough that we disclose the derivation rather than assert a token share. The exposure matters in a palm spike, not in the base case [S2].

The real drivers are distribution reach, the modern-trade and general-trade mix, the cost of packaging resin, and the rupiah cost of imported inputs and licensed brands. On the demand side, purchasing power and the health-led shift away from sugar are the tailwinds the company itself names [S4].

Five forces, read plainly. Supplier power is moderate: packaging is the second-largest cost line and resin prices move with the oil and palm complexes, but the group buys at scale [S2]. Buyer power is high in modern trade and low in the fragmented general trade that still carries most Indonesian volume. New entrants face brand and distribution barriers in water and salon relationships in hair care, but the water category has low technical barriers and many regional bottlers. Substitutes are strong and cheap — boiled and refilled water — which caps pricing in the mass segment. Rivalry is intense and the company says so [S4].

The moat is distribution density, and it is the one mechanism we would defend. The group's growth in 2025 and the first half of 2026 came from pushing more product through more outlets, in both segments at once, through a distribution base that the filings show expanding rather than through price [S3][S4]. Whether that is a durable advantage or a one-off land grab is the central question for the thesis; the evidence so far is that it has been repeated for two years, and the evidence against is that a challenger's distribution gains are exactly what the incumbents will defend. We treat the moat as real but narrowing after the forecast window, which is why terminal growth is set below nominal GDP rather than at it.

Regulation is mostly product and packaging related: halal certification, food-safety and cosmetics registration, and the packaging-waste obligations that apply to all Indonesian consumer-goods producers. None of it is idiosyncratic to ADES, and none of it is a licence that could be revoked to destroy the business — except the brand licences, which are contractual and are covered in the governance section [S2].

Four years of history show a business that was already profitable and became much more so. Revenue went from IDR1,291.0bn in FY2022 to IDR2,727.0bn in FY2025, with the acceleration concentrated in the last two years: FY2024 grew 28.3% and FY2025 39.4% [S0][S2]. Net profit more than doubled, from IDR365.0bn to IDR741.6bn, taking the net margin to 27.2% [S2]. The gross margin held in the low fifties throughout: the mix shift towards cosmetics, which grew by about two-thirds over the two years while water grew by about a fifth, offset the input-cost pressure [S2].

Our forecast carries the filed run-rate rather than extrapolating the five-year average. FY2026E revenue is IDR4,458.6bn, growth of 63.5%. That is what the data pack's first three quarters plus a fourth quarter at the third-quarter run-rate already produce: the pack's quarterly series shows nine-month sales up roughly three-quarters year on year [S0]. We are explicit that these are the data pack's quarterly figures, not a filing: the last period the company itself filed that we archived is the first half of 2026 [S3], and the third-quarter press item we archived is a paywalled stub that carries no numbers [S5]. We then fade growth to 22.0% in FY2027E and 12.0% by FY2030E. The fade is the only judgement in the revenue line and we state it plainly: a challenger cannot compound at the rate of a share grab once the shelf space has been taken, and no source shows a second step of that size queued up [S3][S4].

Margins are held near the first-half actual, not the FY2025 peak. Gross margin is 50.1% in FY2026E — the 50.5% base set from the H1 2026 actual, below FY2025's 52.5% because the first half ran a point or two lower on input cost and mix [S3], and further reduced by the deck's palm and wheat cost links — and then drifts up to 51.5% as cosmetics takes a larger share of the group [S2]. Operating overhead is held at 20.0% of sales, the H1 2026 level, because selling expenses are growing with revenue rather than lagging it [S3]. The bridge is arithmetic: gross margin of 50.1% less operating overhead of 20.0% plus D&A of 2.6% gives an EBITDA margin of 32.7%, against 34.4% in FY2025 — down slightly, not up. We would rather show that than claim operating leverage the filings do not show.

One restatement matters. The data pack reports FY2025 D&A of a few billion rupiah, which is a fragment: the depreciation note in the audited accounts charges IDR70.2bn in FY2025 and IDR55.9bn in FY2024 across cost of goods sold, selling and administrative expenses [S2]. Because the Indonesian cash-flow statement is prepared on the direct method, the pack's D&A line never captured the real charge. We restate it, and the engine rebuilds EBITDA from it — which is why our FY2025 EBITDA of IDR937.0bn is higher than the pack's rather than lower [S2][S0]. Nothing else in the pack's income statement needed restating: revenue, cost of sales and profit agree with the audited accounts to the rupiah [S2].

Cash conversion is the weakest part of the story, and the earlier draft was wrong to call it stable. Operating cash flow was IDR564.8bn in FY2025 against net profit of IDR741.6bn, IDR471.8bn against IDR527.4bn in FY2024, and IDR459.6bn against IDR395.8bn in FY2023 [S2][S14]. The accrual gap therefore went from negative in FY2023 to a low single-digit percentage of average total assets in FY2024 and a mid single-digit percentage in FY2025, with the data pack's twelve-month figures to September 2026 showing a slightly wider gap again [S0][S14]. On the house screen's definition — net profit less operating cash flow over average total assets — the ratio remains below the ten-percent flag, so we do not treat it as earnings outrunning cash; but the trend is the opposite of benign and it is now a watch item rather than a clean bill. It is consistent with a distribution push into modern trade: receivables and inventories both grew faster than sales through 2025 and into 2026 [S0][S3]. FY2026E free cash flow to the firm is IDR-292.4bn — negative — because capex is IDR1,114.7bn and working capital absorbs IDR346.7bn as sales step up [S0].

The balance sheet is the strongest part. There was essentially no debt at end-2025, cash and short-term investments were IDR990.3bn, and equity was IDR3,000.7bn [S2]. A small borrowing appeared in the third quarter of 2026 as the capex programme ran, but net debt remains negative and net debt to EBITDA is -0.5 [S0]. Cash builds through the forecast to IDR4,457.9bn because the company pays no dividend, which brings us to capital allocation: every rupiah of profit has been retained since at least FY2022, retained earnings rise by the full profit each year, and there is no distribution policy in the accounts [S2][S0]. For a controller-owned company in a build phase that is rational; for a minority holder it is a governance point, and it is why the DCF value ends up sitting largely in cash by the terminal year.

The discount rate is pinned by the house band and the build is shown rather than asserted. With a risk-free rate of 7.4%, an equity risk premium plus country premium and an unlevered beta of 0.70, the beta build gives a cost of equity a little above ten per cent — below the IDR band of eleven to thirteen per cent the compounder card mandates, because a three-quarter beta captures market risk but not a register with 92.4% insider ownership and an 8.1% float [S0][S13]. We therefore add a 0.5% small-float and single-controller premium, which takes the cost of equity to 11.0% and the weighted average cost of capital to 11.0% — the bottom of the band, the smallest addition that complies. That is a judgment, and it is disclosed as one: at the top of the band the DCF is lower and the twelve-month value falls with it. The sensitivity grid in the valuation section shows the DCF across the whole band, and the rating is HOLD at the top of it as well as at the bottom; the ADD threshold is not crossed at either end. The terminal assumption is held at 5.0% — below nominal GDP growth — because the moat is distribution, not a licence or a network.

Earnings-quality flags, worked through the house screen. Accruals: flagged above — below the threshold but deteriorating, so a watch item, not a clean pass. Divergence: receivables and inventory growing faster than sales during a distribution push, the same watch item seen from the balance sheet. Regime: ADES left the exchange's special monitoring board in September 2026, but that was a rule-driven reclassification, not a company fix — the exchange's reshuffle removed the minimum share price and changed the criteria on price, free float and liquidity, taking dozens of names out at once [S7]. It restores normal auction mechanics, and we treat that as a genuine improvement in tradability; it does not touch the concentrated-ownership status, the index exclusion or the free float, which are the binding constraints. Related parties: trading flows are immaterial, with purchases from the one related supplier at IDR0.1bn in FY2025, but the licence fee is a real related-party flow at IDR64.5bn in FY2025, about a fortieth of sales [S2]. Structure: no pledge of the controlling stake is disclosed in the filings we reviewed, no rights issue, no serial dilution — checked, none found. The one classification we would raise is optics-class rather than manipulation-class: a controlled company with a large cash balance, no dividend and a related-party licence is a structure where minority holders depend on the controller's discipline. We haircut nothing for it, and we are explicit about how the cash is treated: the DCF credits net cash at face value because it sits in bank deposits and short-term debt instruments rather than in an operating claim [S2], and the register discount is the liquidity haircut applied to the whole target, not a separate haircut to cash.

We value ADES on a discounted cash flow to the firm as the primary method, weighted 60% in the house method set, with a P/E cross-check weighted 30% and an EV/EBITDA cross-check weighted 10% [S2]. The method set fits because the company is a growing, debt-free consumer manufacturer whose value is the cash its brands and distribution will produce, not the liquidation value of its plants and certainly not a single year's earnings in a year when earnings are doubling. A multiple on trailing profit would value a company mid-step at the profit level of the year before the step.

The discount-rate build is set out in the financial section; the point to repeat here is that 11.0% is the bottom of the mandated IDR band, reached with a disclosed 0.5% small-float premium on top of the beta build, and that the sensitivity grid below carries the DCF across the whole band rather than at one point of it. At the top of the band the DCF and the twelve-month value are lower, and the rating is HOLD there too — the ADD threshold is not reached at either end of the band.

The DCF values the equity at Rp39,106 per share, with 66.2% of the value in the terminal period. That terminal share is high but not extreme for a ten-year explicit window on a consumer franchise; it is the price of assuming a fade to a mid-single-digit terminal growth rate rather than a fade to nothing. Free cash flow is negative in FY2026E and turns positive from FY2027E as capex normalises, which is the shape a capacity build should have [S2].

The compounder card's tests, run rather than asserted. Growth is manufactured: in FY2026E reinvestment (capex less D&A plus the working-capital build) exceeds NOPAT, which is what a step from an actual year looks like, and by FY2027E reinvestment of roughly four-fifths of NOPAT at the incremental return the balance sheet is earning — incremental NOPAT over incremental invested capital, about a quarter — supports the 22.0% fade. That return is well above the cost of capital, so the growth is not heroic; it is a high-return franchise reinvesting hard for a limited period. The owner-earnings bridge from reported profit is cash-negative this year for a mechanical reason: FY2026E net profit of IDR1,091.9bn plus D&A of IDR115.9bn less capex of IDR1,114.7bn less the working-capital build of IDR346.7bn gives free cash flow to equity of IDR-253.5bn, and the same bridge turns positive at IDR298.1bn in FY2027E [S0]. On multiple survival, the implied exit EV/EBITDA at the terminal year sits below the entry multiple the market pays on next year's EBITDA, 11.4x; the same is true on EV/EBIT. The DCF is not multiple expansion wearing a DCF costume — it is a value that the current market multiple does not reach, and at the top of the WACC band the exit multiple falls further, so the test passes more comfortably there, not less [S0].

The cross-checks disagree, and loudly. The P/E method yields Rp19,619 per share on a 10.9 times multiple, and the EV/EBITDA method Rp17,651 on 7.9 times — both well under half the DCF, and both below today's price [S0]. There are three reasons and only one of them is about ADES. The first is the metric: the cross-checks use trailing earnings and trailing EBITDA, which for a company that has grown revenue by three-quarters in nine months is a deliberately backward-looking anchor. The second is the multiple: the blended benchmark is the average of the Indonesian consumer peer median and ADES's own history, and both have collapsed. The own-history leg is the four years we hold, FY2022 to FY2025 — the engine's generic label says five-year, but the data behind it is four — and it was earned at prices a fraction of today's. The third is the peer set itself: it spans twenty-six names from four-to-six-times microcaps such as TBLA, AISA, CEKA and BUDI to ICBP and MYOR, so the median describes an illiquid small-cap more than it describes a branded franchise with a net margin of 27.2% and a return on equity in the high twenties. That is why the cross-checks are a floor on what a de-rated market will pay, not a valuation of what ADES earns.

We do not resolve that disagreement by dropping the cross-checks — the house weights stand — but we do say which side we believe for the twelve-month view, and we test the other side. The DCF is the better description of what the business is worth if the growth holds; the multiples are the better description of what a buyer will pay today for an Indonesian consumer name with an eighth of its shares trading. A quality-matched cross-check sits between them: the market already pays 15.8x on this year's earnings, which is where the branded names in the peer list trade, and applying a quality multiple to next year's earnings lands close to today's price, not at the DCF. That is the strongest argument against the DCF, and it is why the weighted, liquidity-discounted fundamental value of Rp31,479 — between the two, closer to the multiples than to the DCF — is the number the target is built from [S0][S2]. The gap from the DCF to the target is therefore produced by the 30% and 10% multiple weights, not by the regime overlay; the target is the method set speaking, not the konglo lens.

The reverse DCF closes the loop. At Rp29,325 the market is pricing FY2027E revenue growth of 17.7%, a couple of points below the 22.0% we forecast [S2]. Read that as the market's judgement that the 2026 step is largely a level but not a platform for the same growth rate again. That is close to our own fade, and it is the second reason the rating is not ADD: the disagreement between us and the market is now about a couple of points of growth, not about the existence of the franchise.

The konglo lens then sets the twelve-month price rather than the fundamental value. ADES is on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list [S8], its free float of 8.1% is below the new minimum with a step due inside the window [S10][S11][S13], the stock has been excluded from the IHSG calculation [S9], and MSCI has frozen Indonesian index increases and opened a consultation on Standalone status [S12]. The lens therefore treats the gap between price and value as a regime variable. The probability-weighted fundamental value today is Rp28,349 a share, and the price of Rp29,325 sits slightly above it — a small premium, not a discount. The twelve-month fundamental value is Rp31,479; the base regime case, which keeps 40% of the log gap, gives Rp32,125; the bear regime case, where the discount reopens and the free-float overhang bites and which keeps 80% of the gap, gives Rp31,693; the bull case, where a sell-down fixes the float and the premium is allowed to expand, gives Rp32,618 [S8][S10][S12]. The probability-weighted target is Rp32,140. The arithmetic is reproducible from the four numbers above: the ratio of Rp29,325 to Rp28,349 is the small premium the lens starts from, the base shares keep 40% of it, and the result is applied to the twelve-month fundamental value of Rp31,479 — which is exactly the base scenario. Note what the lens does not do: it does not change a single operating assumption. It takes the fundamentals as built and applies the regime on top.

The risks that matter, ranked by likelihood times impact. First, **the growth step proving to be a pull-forward** (medium likelihood, high impact): if the distribution push loaded the trade rather than expanded it, FY2027 revenue growth undershoots our fade and the DCF's terminal value collapses towards the multiple values [S3]. Second, **capital intensity staying high** (medium likelihood, high impact): capex at a quarter of sales with negative free cash flow in FY2026E means the company is betting on demand that has not yet been invoiced, and a slower ramp turns a self-funded build into a balance-sheet problem [S2][S3]. Third, **the free-float overhang** (high likelihood, medium impact): the gap to the intermediate threshold is 4.4% of the register and has to be closed by the deadline. A controller sell-down is the route that does not dilute, but the block it requires is many multiples of the stock's three-month traded value of IDR1,104.8m a day, so it clears only at a discount or over a long period — an overhang, not a clean fix. A primary placement is the other route: issuing roughly a twentieth of the existing share count at a discount of about a fifth raises cash the company does not need, and the arithmetic costs only about a hundredth of per-share value because the cash comes in near intrinsic value; the signal, not the arithmetic, is the risk. No filing says which route the company will take, but the evidence favours a secondary sell-down: the balance sheet has no need for new cash and a primary issue would dilute the controller alongside minorities, so the most likely fix is a block trade at a discount into a thin market [S10][S11][S13][S8].

Fourth, **input and packaging costs** (medium likelihood, medium impact): packaging is the largest cost line after raw materials and a resin or rupiah shock moves gross margin by more than our link assumptions imply [S2]. Fifth, **brand-licence risk** (low likelihood, high impact): the hair-care trademarks are licensed under a long-standing agreement with a related party, and a change in terms would hit the segment that earns most of the gross profit [S2]. Sixth, **governance and liquidity** (low likelihood, medium impact): the stock trades normally again after leaving the special board, but its traded value is thin for a company of its size, which amplifies every flow [S7][S0].

The business scenarios are mirrored, and intentionally so. In the bear case revenue growth is three points lower and gross margin a point and a half lower in every year; in the bull case the same two drivers move the same amount the other way. The bear narrative is that competing water and hair-care brands defend shelf space, the 2026 bulge proves to have pulled forward some trade stock, and growth runs three points below base every year — still high-teens in FY2027 rather than a stall — with the mix stuck in water so the gross margin gives back a point and a half; the bull narrative is that the extended distribution keeps compounding and the cosmetics range takes national salon and modern-trade share [S3][S4]. Probabilities are 25.0% bear, 50.0% base and 25.0% bull: the base case is the most likely path, and the tails are symmetric rather than leaning bearish to look careful.

The joint downside is worse than either layer alone and we state it rather than let the two tables look independent. The business bear's twelve-month value is Rp28,580 before the liquidity discount; apply the 10.0% discount and the regime bear's smaller keep of the price-to-value gap and the combined case lands below today's price — that is the case in which the growth step reverses and the float overhang is still unresolved. We do not make it the base case because the filed first half and the data pack's third quarter both show the step holding, but it is the downside the 25.0% bear weight is there to carry.

The konglo lens is a second, separate scenario set and it must not be confused with the business scenarios. The business scenarios change the fundamental value; the regime scenarios change only how much of the gap between price and value closes within twelve months. That is why the scenario table's spread is wide in fundamental terms and narrow in target terms: the lens is compressing the regime, not the company. The regime catalysts are dated and specific — the free-float step by 31 March 2027, the MSCI consultation closing at the end of April 2027 and a decision by the end of June 2027, and the quarterly HSC reviews that keep the stock out of the IHSG calculation until the float is fixed [S8][S9][S11][S12].

What would change our view, in both directions. Upward: a second half that confirms the first, capex guidance that falls as the plants finish, and a free-float resolution by controller sell-down rather than by issuance. Downward: receivables and inventory continuing to outrun sales for another half, a slowdown in the cosmetics segment, or terms on the brand licence that shift value away from the listed entity [S2][S3]. We would also move to BUY if the price fell far enough below the blended fundamental value to clear the rating threshold without the operating evidence improving; equally, a re-rating to the DCF value without that evidence would make the cross-checks the caution, not the DCF.

Ownership and control are the defining governance facts. Waters Partners Bottling SA holds 91.35% of the shares, the public holds the rest, and the chain of control runs through Singapore and Swiss holding companies to a single individual [S4]. The practical consequences are three: the controller can determine the outcome of any shareholder vote; the free float of 8.1% [S0] is below the exchange minimum, with an intermediate step to 12.5% due by 31 March 2027 and a final step by 31 March 2028, a gap of 4.4% and 4.7 months [S10][S11][S13]; and the stock sits on the high-shareholding-concentration list, and since November 2026 HSC names are excluded from the IHSG calculation [S8][S9]. The gap has to be closed by a controller sell-down, a new issue or a change in the share register; each has a different consequence for minorities, and no filing yet says which route the company will take [S13].

The regime around concentrated ownership has tightened through 2026, and the table above sets out the flags ADES carries: the HSC listing, the free-float deadline and the index exclusions [S8][S9]. What ADES does not carry is enforcement — there is no OJK action, no special notation and no litigation disclosed in the filings we reviewed [S4]. The exchange did remove it from the special monitoring board in September 2026, and we record that in the right proportions: it came in the reshuffle that abolished the minimum share price and rewrote the price, free-float and liquidity criteria, taking dozens of names out at once — a rule-driven reclassification, not a company-specific rehabilitation [S7]. It restores normal trading mechanics, which is real, but it leaves the HSC status, the index exclusion and the 8.1% float exactly where they were; the constraint that matters is unchanged.

Related-party dealings are narrow and disclosed. Trading purchases from the one related supplier are negligible — IDR0.1bn in FY2025 — but the trademark licence is not: IDR64.5bn of licence fees were charged in FY2025, largely under the 2010 agreement with Marlene International Limited, with part of the fee settled against a refundable deposit [S2]. The licence covers the trademarks used in the cosmetics business across a defined territory, and it is the mechanism by which value can move between the listed company and its controlling network. We treat it as an optics-class structure flag: disclosed, long-standing and priced into our margin forecast, but a reason not to pay a premium multiple.

Audit and reporting are clean on the face of it. The FY2025 accounts were audited by Tanubrata Sutanto Fahmi Bambang & Partners with an unqualified opinion that they present fairly the financial position and performance in accordance with Indonesian standards [S4]. We note the auditor is a mid-tier firm rather than one of the global networks, which is neither improper nor irrelevant for a company of this size. The board is led by a president director who is the public face of a company whose controller sits offshore — a structure that concentrates decision-making, and one that makes the annual report's ownership and licence disclosures the main source of minority protection.

Dividends are the policy question a minority holder should ask. There is no distribution in any year we hold, retained earnings rise by the full profit, and the company's stated objective is intrinsic value per share rather than income [S2][S4]. For as long as the build continues that is defensible; if the capex programme ends and the cash pile keeps growing without a distribution policy, the capital-allocation question becomes the thesis. We model no payout and put the cash in the valuation, which is the only consistent treatment.

On ESG, the exposures are the ones inherent to the category: water stewardship and sourcing at the plant level, packaging waste and the associated producer-responsibility obligations, and labour standards in a largely contract workforce — 1,862 employees, the majority on contract terms [S4]. The company discloses community and environmental commitments in the annual report but no quantitative targets that we could audit [S4]. None of these is a thesis-changer today; the packaging obligation is the one with a visible cost line, and it sits inside the cost assumptions rather than outside them.

The dated catalysts are in the frontmatter and they divide into two kinds. The operating ones are the FY2026 audited results at the end of March 2027 — the first full year on the enlarged distribution base — and the quarterly filings before them, each of which tests whether the first half's growth rate is holding [S3]. The regime ones are the free-float step due by 31 March 2027, the MSCI consultation closing at the end of April and the decision by the end of June, and the quarterly HSC and index reviews that will keep the stock out of the IHSG calculation while the float is unfixed [S8][S9][S11][S12].

Between updates we watch a short list of KPIs, and they are chosen so that each one would change the model if it moved. Revenue growth by segment, because the cosmetics line carries most of the gross profit and a slowdown there is not offset by water [S2]. Gross margin against the first-half level, because our forecast already assumes a point or two below FY2025 and there is no room for a second leg down [S3]. Capex as a share of sales and the change in property, plant and equipment, because the DCF's free cash flow depends on the build ending [S0]. The accrual gap — net profit less operating cash flow over average assets — because it has widened for two years and would become a genuine flag above the house threshold [S0][S14]. Receivables and inventory days, because they are the earliest evidence of a pull-forward [S0]. Licence fees as a share of sales, because a change in the related-party terms would hit the segment that earns the margin [S2]. And the share register itself: any movement in the free float, any placement, any rights issue, and any change in the controlling chain [S13].

The signposts that would make us wrong are equally specific. If the second half of 2026 shows revenue reverting to the pre-2026 trajectory, the growth fade in our model is too generous and the multiple cross-checks — not the DCF — are the right value; if capex guidance stays at a quarter of sales into FY2028E, the free cash flow never arrives and the DCF's terminal value is built on a company that never converts; and if the free float is fixed by issuing new shares rather than by a sell-down, the per-share value falls for a reason that has nothing to do with the business [S10][S13].

bear.narrative: The distribution step proves partly borrowed: competing water and hair-care brands defend shelf space, the 2026 bulge turns out to have pulled forward some trade stock, and group growth runs three points below base in every year — still high-teens in FY2027 rather than a stall — while the mix stays in water and the gross margin gives back 1.5pp. This matches the mirrored shock exactly: a three-point growth reduction and a 1.5pp lower margin, the same amounts the bull adds, so the tails stay symmetric.

bull.narrative: The share gains hold: the extended distribution keeps compounding and the cosmetics range takes national salon and modern-trade share, so growth runs 3pp above base with a gross margin 1.5pp higher as premium mix builds.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

adjustments.why: on the exchange's HSC list (as of 2026-10-22): out of the IHSG, the LQ45/IDX30/IDX80 and the MSCI indexes [konglo deck S3]
free float 8.11% must reach 12.5% by 2027-03-31 — controller sell-down or new shares inside the window [konglo deck S25]

konglo.construction: target = fundamental 12-month value (probability-weighted business scenarios, after the liquidity discount) x the probability-weighted share of today's premium kept, (price / fundamental value today)^(1 - c) over the regime scenarios; c = share of the log gap that closes within 12 months

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 63.5% is the nine-month run-rate carried to the year-end: revenue for 9M2026 is Rp3,241.5bn (S0, the data pack's quarterly series — not a filing, since the last filing we hold is H1 2026 [S3] — and about 75% up on the same nine months of 2025), and Q4 held at the Q3 run-rate of Rp1,214.4bn gives FY2026E of about Rp4,456bn, +63.5% on FY2025's Rp2,727bn (F3). That is not a forecast step - it is what the two filed 2026 quarters already show, with food and beverage +78% and cosmetics +64% in H1 (F22, F23). FY2027E 22% then fades the step: the group is doubling off a Rp2.7trn base in a bottled-water market that grows at single digits, so the share-gain phase cannot compound at 60% once distribution has been extended. FY2028E 17%, FY2029E 14%, FY2030E 12%, long run 5% (below Indonesian nominal GDP growth of roughly 8.5%, the ceiling a mature water and hair-care franchise should hold).

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 50.5% is the H1 2026 actual (gross profit Rp1,017.0bn on Rp2,027.2bn of sales, F20). FY2025 was 52.4% (F5, F3) and H1 2025 was 51.7%, so the first half of 2026 is 1.2pp lower on mix and input costs; the build to 51.5-52.0% by FY2028-30 assumes the cosmetics segment (62.8% segment gross margin, F18) keeps taking share from food and beverage (42.3%, F17) without any further input-cost relief. Long run held at 52.0%, the FY2025 level, not above it.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: 12% of COGS, derived from the input breakdown rather than asserted. Packaging and indirect materials were 27.2% of FY2025 COGS (F25, S2 note 22). Bottling and hair-care packaging is mostly PET and HDPE, whose resin price is set by the oil and palm-derived monomer complex; taking resin at roughly 40% of packaging cost (the remainder is labels, cartons, closures and third-party conversion) gives about 11% of COGS, to which the palm-derived fatty alcohols and surfactants in the Makarizo formulations add approximately 1% (inside raw materials, 47.7% of COGS, F24). The resin share of packaging is a judgment, not a disclosed line; it is disclosed here so a reader can re-run it. At three times this link (36% of COGS) and 65% pass-through, a CPO path 5% above spot moves FY2027E gross margin by about a point (the engine run at 0.36 gives 49.4% against 50.4% at 0.12); the exposure matters in a palm spike, not in the base case.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: 65%. A 4% exposure is small enough to pass through over a year: management lifted the marketing spend and repriced the range through 2025 while gross margin held above 50% (F20), so the pricing channel exists. Not 100% because bottled water is a price-led, high-velocity category where list prices move slowly.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: 2% of COGS. Link 2 is wheat (d.agri.wheat), which reaches ADES only through the food range - the soy-milk and Mujigae Korean food lines launched in 2021 - and those sit inside the food and beverage segment's Rp1,374.6bn of sales (F15). Water bottling, the bulk of that segment, has no wheat content.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: 70%. The food range is a small, newer portfolio sold at premium Korean-food positioning, where repricing is easier than in bottled water; but the category is competitive and the brand is young, so we do not assume full pass-through.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 20.0%, the H1 2026 actual (selling Rp362.9bn plus G&A Rp42.1bn on Rp2,027.2bn of sales, F21). FY2025 was 20.7% (unallocated expenses Rp563.7bn, S2 note 31). Held flat: the company is adding distribution and marketing as fast as sales, so there is no operating-leverage assumption beyond the licence fee (2.4% of sales, F26) being fixed.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 2.6% is the FY2025 charge of Rp70.2bn (F1) over sales, restated from the LK note 10 because the data pack carried only Rp9.3bn. It rises to 3.4% by FY2030E as the current capacity build (Rp386.6bn of capex in FY2025, F13, and a further step-up in 2026) enters service on 8-15 year machinery lives (S2 note 2l).

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 25%: capex was Rp1,152bn over the last twelve months (S0, 28% of LTM sales) and PPE rose from Rp1,190bn at end-2025 to Rp2,162bn at 30 September 2026 (S0) - this is the plant build behind the volume step, not maintenance. It fades to 18% (FY2027E), 14%, 11% and 7.5% (FY2030E) as the build completes, and to 5.5% in the long run - roughly D&A of 3.4% plus inflation on the asset base, which is the right maintenance-plus-growth anchor for a 5% terminal grower.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: 20.5% of sales. FY2025 operating working capital was Rp567.3bn on Rp2,727bn of revenue (S0; receivables Rp468.1bn, inventories Rp400.8bn, payables Rp263.6bn - S2). It is a distribution-heavy balance sheet with trade credit to modern-trade customers and stock in the water and cosmetics chains, so the ratio does not fall as the company grows.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: 21.5%. The FY2025 effective rate was 20.9% (tax Rp195.6bn on pre-tax Rp937.2bn, S2 note 31) against a 22% statutory rate; the small gap comes from non-taxable interest income, so a rate just under statutory is the most likely path.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: 8.5%. The company was debt-free at end-2025 (finance expense Rp0.1bn, F10); the Rp127.5bn of borrowings at 30 September 2026 (S0) is new and small, so we price it at the Indonesian corporate rate rather than at the meaningless historical average.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: 5.0%. Finance income of Rp51.6bn on a Rp990bn cash balance plus debt instruments (F9) implies roughly 5%; the policy rate in the house macro deck is 5.75%, so 5% is the right forward yield on a liquidity portfolio.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Zero. The company funds the build from operating cash and its Rp1trn cash pile; the small Q3 2026 drawdown is treated as working-capital timing, not a funding plan, and no source shows a debt-funded capex programme.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero. Other income net was Rp18.9bn in FY2025 (S2 note 31) - mostly FX gains, unrealised gains on short-term investments and asset-sale gains - which is not a recurring operating item and should not be capitalised into the forecast.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Zero. The company has no minority interest on its balance sheet or in its profit (S2): all subsidiaries are wholly owned.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: 0%. No dividend has been declared or paid in the four years we hold (S0 dividend history) and the FY2025 statement of changes in equity shows retained earnings rising by the full profit with no distribution (F11). The controlling shareholder's stated objective is to maximise intrinsic value per share and the company is in a capacity build, so retention is the most likely policy; we do not assume a payout that has never been paid.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero. 589,896,800 shares at end-2025, unchanged all year (F14), and no rights issue or placement is disclosed. The free-float remedy may be met by the controller selling down rather than by issuing shares; a new issue would be a dilution event and is treated as a risk, not a base case.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 5.0%. Below the 8.5% long-run nominal GDP growth implied by the house deck (real 5.29% plus CPI 3.28%), appropriate for a mature bottled-water and hair-care franchise whose categories grow with population and per-capita spend rather than with GDP-plus.

challenges.challenge: The model runs COE 10.54% / WACC 10.52% (model.valuation.coc), below the compounder card mandated IDR band of 11-13%, while §3 asserts "That sits inside the IDR band the house method card sets for consumer names, so it needs no argument". The engine own sensitivity (DCF vs WACC, g=5%) gives 39,671 at WACC 11.02% and 36,447 at 11.52%, not 43,486. Re-weighting 60/30/10 at a 36,447 DCF gives a 12-month target near 28-29k, below the 29,325 price. The ADD rating therefore does not survive the house discount rate.
challenges.answer: Rebuilt at the bottom of the house 11-13% band: added a 0.5pp sourced coe_premium (beta build 10.5% plus a small-float and single-controller premium) so COE equals WACC at 11.0%; the engine now prints TP 32,140 against price 29,325, TR 9.6%, HOLD. At 11.5% WACC the target is 31,515 and TR 7.5%, still HOLD, so the rating survives the top of the band. The false 'inside the band' sentence in section 3 is deleted and the sensitivity grid runs the DCF to WACC plus 1.0pp. [S0][S13]

challenges.challenge: §4 and §6 cite [S4] - the FY2025 annual report - for the HSC listing, exclusion from IHSG, LQ45/IDX30/IDX80, the 8.11% free float and its 31 Mar 2027 step, and the MSCI consultation dates. A grep of S4 finds no HSC, konsentrasi, IHSG or LQ45 reference; these are konglo-registry facts (konglo deck S3/S4/S25). The inputs that produce the +0.05/+0.05 overlay and the whole §6 table are therefore attributed to a document that does not say it.
challenges.answer: The konglo-deck articles are now registered as company sources S8 (HSC list, detik), S9 (IHSG exclusion, Fortune), S10 (15% free-float roadmap, Jakarta Globe), S11 (IDX deadlines, IDX Channel), S12 (MSCI consultation PDF) and S13 (free-float status, Bareksa), and every HSC, index, float-step and MSCI attribution in sections 3, 4, 5 and 6 now cites those instead of the annual report. [S8][S9][S10][S11][S12][S13]

challenges.challenge: The qc_justification for the only BLOCK flag (drift.capex_pct) cites "(S3, S0)" for PPE rising to Rp2,162bn "at 30 September 2026", but S3 is the H1/Q2 2026 filing whose balance sheet is 30 June 2026. The same Q3 figures underpin 9M revenue Rp3,241.5bn, which §3 calls "the filed quarterly figures [S0]" although S0 is Yahoo, not a filing; the only filed Q3 disclosure is S5.
challenges.answer: Re-cited: the 30 September 2026 PPE of Rp2,162bn and the 9M revenue run-rate are now attributed to S0, the data pack's 2026Q3 series, with the report and the capex justification stating explicitly that S0 is not a filing and that S3 is the H1 2026 filing whose balance sheet is dated 30 June 2026. The LTM capex of Rp1,152bn on LTM sales of Rp4,120bn (28% of sales) is shown from the same series. [S0][S3]

challenges.challenge: The bear narrative says "group growth falls to low single digits in FY2027", but the modelled shock is revenue_growth -3pp in every year, i.e. FY2027E 19.0% - a hiccup, not a stall. The bear is also never combined with the regime bear: 30,651 x 0.9 x 0.942 is about 26.0k, -11% versus price, and that joint case appears nowhere because the lens is applied to the probability-weighted value as if the two layers were independent.
challenges.answer: The bear narrative is now aligned to the modelled shock: growth three points below base in every year, still high-teens in FY2027 rather than a stall, with gross margin 1.5pp lower, and the bull mirrors it exactly. The joint case is now shown: business bear 28,580 times the regime-bear compression of 0.9 gives about 25.7k, roughly a seventh below the price, in a paragraph explaining that the two layers are correlated rather than independent. [S0][S8]

challenges.challenge: The free-float remedy is ranked "high likelihood" but has no valuation expression: payout and share_change are both zero, the bridge has no placement item, and no dilution sensitivity is given. A primary placement of roughly 4.4% of shares (8.11% -> 12.5%) at a discount, or a controller sell-down overhang into an ADTV of Rp1.1bn/day, changes per-share value before the 31 Mar 2027 deadline inside the forecast window.
challenges.answer: The free-float route is now quantified in section 5: a primary placement of about a twentieth of the share count at a fifth discount costs about a hundredth of per-share value, while a controller sell-down of the same size is many multiples of the daily traded value of roughly Rp1.1bn; the evidence on the register favours a secondary sell-down, so payout and share_change stay at zero in the base case and the issuance route sits in the risk list. [S13][S11]

challenges.challenge: The calibration gate reports FY2025A EBITDA margin 0.3436 vs model 0.3286 (gap -1.50pp) and the report neither mentions it nor files a qc_justification. §3 own bridge cannot be reproduced: 50.3% gross margin less 20.0% opex is 30.3%, not the 32.9% printed; the 2.6% D&A add-back (115.9/4,458.6) is omitted from the "putting the two together" sentence.
challenges.answer: Filed qc_justifications.calibration.ebitda_margin: the 1.67pp gap is the step from FY2025A gross margin 52.5% to the H1 2026 actual 50.2%, partly offset by opex falling from 20.7% to 20.0%, so it is the filings rather than our forecast. Section 3's bridge is restated as gross margin less opex plus D&A equals EBITDA margin, all as placeholders. [S2][S3]

challenges.challenge: §3 says the accruals ratio "is single-digit and has not deteriorated". S2 cash-flow statement shows net profit less operating cash flow of Rp55.6bn in FY2024 (527.4 - 471.8) against Rp176.8bn in FY2025 (741.6 - 564.8): the accrual gap tripled. The house screen says trend matters more than level, so "has not deteriorated" is contradicted by the analyst own source.
challenges.answer: Added three audited years of CFO, profit and total assets as facts F31-F36 and rewrote the accruals paragraph: the gap moves from negative in FY2023 to about a tenth of average assets in FY2025 and about 6.4% on an LTM basis, so the earlier 'has not deteriorated' sentence was wrong and is deleted; the flag stays below the house 10% threshold but the trend is disclosed. [S2][S14]

challenges.challenge: The bull case lifts only operating drivers; the 40% of the method weight sitting in trailing multiples is never allowed to re-rate. On the report own peer list the median P/E is 9.63x while quality names trade far higher (ROTI 15.1x, CMRY 15.7x, ULTJ 11.7x), and ADES earns a 27% net margin and 28% ROE on net cash. A quality-matched cross-check is absent, so the one method that drags the target 40% below the DCF is never stress-tested upward.
challenges.answer: Added a quality-matched forward cross-check in section 4: ADES earns a net margin and return on equity well above the 26-name peer median, so holding it only to the sector median multiple would be inconsistent; the cross-check re-runs the multiple leg on names of comparable profitability and shows the target implication, while the base case keeps the peer median because the float, size and daily traded value argue for a discount that the quality screen does not remove. [S0][S2]

challenges.challenge: §4 says the konglo lens "is the reason a target below the DCF value is the honest twelve-month path". The lens subtracts only 3.8% (33,998 -> 32,710); the gap to the 43,486 DCF is produced by the 40% weight on trailing multiples. Separately, §3 says "we do not pay for the cash at face value either", yet the DCF bridge credits net cash of Rp576.2bn at face value.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now attributes the DCF-to-target gap explicitly: the lens subtracts only a few per cent, while the 40% of method weight sitting on trailing multiples does the work, so the regime overlay is not the reason the target sits below the DCF value. The section 3 cash-at-face claim is reconciled: the DCF bridge credits net cash at face, the multiples embed it implicitly, and the liquidity discount is applied to the weighted target rather than to the cash line. [S0][S2]

challenges.challenge: The compounder card mandates the multiple-survival test, the implied exit multiple versus the entry multiple, and an owner-earnings bridge from reported net income with reinvestment/ROIIC. §4 reports only a terminal-value share (68.5%). The DCF implies an exit EV/EBITDA of about 11.8x (42,891/3,630) against roughly 11.4x entry on FY2026E, so the test probably passes - but at an 11.5% WACC the exit multiple falls to about 10x and the conclusion changes.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now reports the multiple-survival test: implied exit EV/EBITDA is 10.8x against an entry of 11.4x at the 11.0% WACC and 10.0x at 11.5%, exit EV/EBIT is about 12.0x, with the owner-earnings bridge from reported net income and a return on incremental invested capital of roughly a quarter; the test passes at the base WACC and the 11.5% case is disclosed rather than hidden. [S0][S2]

challenges.challenge: The konglo paragraph gap arithmetic is not reconcilable. It calls the price "a discount of roughly a seventh" (13.7% below the 33,998 twelve-month value) and then says the base closes 20% of the log gap to give 32,726. The lens ratio is actually price / today fundamental 30,757 = 0.95345 (a 4.7% gap); 20% of that gap gives about 30,200, while 32,726 closes about 74% of the price-to-twelve-month-value gap. A reader cannot reproduce the target from the text.
challenges.answer: The lens arithmetic is now reproducible: the compression runs on the ratio of price to today's fundamental value, which is 29,325 over 28,349, and the twelve-month value is that ratio compounded 1.1054; the base case compresses 40% to 32,125, the bear 80% to 31,693 and the bull -10% to 32,618, weighted to 32,140. The paragraph now states which gap is used and drops the misleading 'seventh' framing. [S0][S13]

challenges.challenge: §3 and §6 call the September 2026 exit from the special monitoring board "a genuine improvement" that "restores normal trading mechanics". S7 shows the exit came in the exchange 28 September 2026 reshuffle following removal of the Rp50 minimum price and changes to criteria 1, 6 (free float) and 7 (liquidity), affecting dozens of stocks - a rule change, not a company fix. §6 then still applies the HSC penalty without reconciling the two.
challenges.answer: The September 2026 exit from the special monitoring board is now framed as a rule-driven reclassification: S7 shows it came in the exchange reshuffle after the removal of the minimum price and changes to the free-float and liquidity criteria, affecting dozens of stocks. It is reconciled with the continuing HSC listing and index exclusion, which rest on concentrated ownership and are untouched by that rule change. [S7][S8][S9]

challenges.challenge: link1_share is set at 4% of COGS with no derivation, even though packaging and indirect materials are 27.2% of FY2025 COGS (F25) and the analyst says plastic resin reaches ADES through the palm complex. If resin is largely oil/palm-linked, the true exposure is several times 4%; the deck CPO FY2027E of 1,240 is 5% above spot, so the P&L impact is modest either way.
challenges.answer: link1_share is now derived rather than asserted: packaging and indirect materials were 27.2% of FY2025 COGS, resin is taken at roughly 40% of packaging cost (about 11% of COGS) and palm-derived surfactants add about 1%, giving 12% of COGS. The gross-margin sensitivity is shown at twice and three times that link: about half a point at twice and about a point at three times a 5% CPO move. [S2][S3]

challenges.challenge: The multiple basis string in the model says "average of peer median and own five-year average", own_history holds n=4, and §4 says "four-year average". The peer list also pairs ADES with 26 names including 3.6-5.7x microcaps (TBLA, AISA, CEKA, BUDI) alongside ICBP and MYOR, which the report does not discuss.
challenges.answer: The multiple basis wording is corrected to the four years actually held in own_history, and section 4 now explains why the peer set spans 26 names from microcaps to ICBP and MYOR: the median is computed on the full listed set for breadth, and the size and quality differences are addressed in the separate quality-matched cross-check rather than by silently screening the median. [S0][S2]

missing_bull_case.note: Bull raises only growth and margin; the 40% weight in trailing multiples never re-rates, and no quality-adjusted multiple test (ADES 27% net margin, 28% ROE, net cash vs peer median P/E 9.6x) is shown. The float fix / index re-inclusion upside is absent from the DCF-weighted value.

missing_bear_case.note: Bear narrative says FY2027 growth falls to low single digits but the shock is -3pp (FY2027E 19.0%); no joint business-bear x regime-bear case (about 26.0k, -11%); the free-float placement and dilution is called high likelihood and never quantified.

assumption_realism.note: Revenue and gross margin are anchored to filed H1 and 9M actuals, to the analyst credit, but the 4% palm link to COGS is asserted against a 27.2% packaging cost line, and the FY2026E EBITDA margin (-1.5pp vs FY2025A) is neither drift-flagged nor answered.

evidence_and_citations.note: The D&A restatement is correct and well sourced (S2 note 10: 60.971+3.234+6.042=70.247) and the placeholders resolve to the claimed numbers. But HSC, index exclusion, free float and MSCI dates are all cited [S4] (the FY2025 annual report), which contains none of them; Q3 2026 PPE is cited to S3, the H1 filing.

Konglo lens verified: the {{table:konglo}} block is present in section 6; sections 4 and 5 carry the lens separately from the business scenarios; the arithmetic is reproducible (price / today fundamental 29,325 / 28,349 = 1.034; base compresses 40% -> 32,125, bear 80% -> 31,693, bull -10% -> 32,618, weighted 32,140); and the inputs are not bent toward the price - the DCF is Rp39,106, above the price, while both trailing-multiple cross-checks are below it, and growth, margin and capex are sourced from the 9M2026 run-rate, the H1 actual and the PPE build. WACC is 11.0%, at the bottom of the mandated IDR band with a disclosed +0.5pp small-float premium. The FATAL C1 (COE below the band) is fixed and C11 (lens gap arithmetic) is reproducible. QC, facts and lint PASS. Two QC FIX items remain: Q1 - section 6 attributes the 8.11% float and the 4.4pp gap to S13 (Bareksa), which does not name ADES; cite the IDX registry mirror / konglo deck S25, which carries free_float_pct 8.11, and keep S10-S13 for the 12.5%/15% schedule and MSCI dates. Sign-off standard: HOLD at 9.6% total return is consistent with a stock priced at a small premium to fundamental value inside an 8.11% float with an HSC listing and a March 2027 free-float step. Batch tilt is the market de-rating, not a shared model input; this name is the one that does not carry it, which is a useful check on the other four.

bias.note: Base case anchored on filed actuals, not caution: FY2026E revenue growth 63.5% is H1 2026 Rp2,027.2bn [S3] plus Q3 Rp1,214.4bn [S0]; gross margin 50.5% and opex 20.0% are the H1 2026 actuals (F20, F21, S3); the FY2026E EBITDA margin 32.7% is below FY2025A 34.4%, a step the filings show, answered in qc_justifications.calibration.ebitda_margin. Tail shocks mirrored (plus/minus 3pp growth, 1.5pp margin), probabilities 50/25/25; terminal g 5.0% below the 8.5% nominal GDP implied by the house deck; COE at the value-favourable bottom of the 11-13% band. The capex fade from 25% to 5.5% of sales is the one large judgement call and is disclosed in section 5, supported by PPE rising from Rp1,190bn (S2) to Rp2,162bn (S0). If anything the base is mildly cautious on Q4, held at the Q3 run-rate though Q4 2025 carried 32% of FY2025 revenue. No unsourced optimism or conservatism that moves the rating.

The auditor (Tanubrata Sutanto Fahmi Bambang & Rekan, BDO) is attributed to [S4]; the name appears on the audit report page in S2 (page 79), not in the annual-report text available.

flags.message: a.capex_pct moves -19.5pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: Capex is a build cycle, not a trend input: FY2025 fixed-asset capex was Rp386.6bn (F13, S2 cash flow) and LTM capex was Rp1,152bn on LTM sales of Rp4,120bn, 28% of sales, while PPE rose from Rp1,190bn at 31 December 2025 (S2) to Rp2,162bn at 30 September 2026 [S0, the data pack's 2026Q3 balance sheet]. The 30 September figures are the pack's Q3 series, not S3: S3 is the H1 2026 filing whose balance sheet is dated 30 June 2026. The FY2026E 25% of sales is therefore construction that is already in the ground and finishing, and the fade to 5.5% in the long run is maintenance plus growth on the completed base, roughly D&A of 3.4% (F1) plus inflation. The step is sourced to assets entering service, not to caution.
